tooltip.recompile.animal_bait: Place on grass and step away - wildlife will not come while you are near. Keep baits apart.
jei.recompile.info.motor: Salvaged from Mechanical Waste in the demolition yard. It turns nothing on its own - it is a part, and the Separator is built around one. No amount of scrap makes a working motor.
jei.recompile.info.bulb: Found in household sorting. The Hydroponics Bay needs one: a bay built under a mound has no other light.
container.recompile.take_hint: Click 1, Shift a stack, Right-click half
jade.recompile.compost_empty: Empty - feed it muck or fiber
jade.recompile.trommel_feed: Feed: drop scrap on the drum, or set a container on it
jade.recompile.workbench_empty: Rack a Scrap Knife or Prybar
jade.recompile.workbench_ready: Hold right-click to break it down
jei.recompile.info.compost_heap: A 2x2x2 salvage cage that composts the dump's organics into Fertilizer. Place the core and build the cage from seven Machine Frames. Feed it any compostable - Organic Muck, Fiber Scrap, or plant matter like leaves, saplings, grass, crops and seeds: every few forms a layer, each layer ripens on its own, and a finished layer is right-clicked out for one Fertilizer. It never has to be full.
jei.recompile.info.fertilizer: Finished compost from the Compost Heap. Right-click reclaimed grass to scatter weeds and wildflowers across it - rung 2 of bringing the world back - or right-click mycelium to grow mushrooms. It does nothing on the raw dump, so heal the ground with a Grass Spreader first. The plants it grows are torn out by the encroaching dump before it takes the grass, so a fertilized border holds a little longer.
jei.recompile.info.grass_spreader: Waters the ground around it, turning coarse dirt and dirt to grass one block at a time. Build up from the core: Water Tank, Pump, Solar Panel on top, and a Copper Pipe on each side of the Pump. It sits idle until the whole tower is up.
jei.recompile.info.rain_collector: Rain is the only source of fresh water in this world. Put a Rain Collector Funnel on top and leave it under open sky. Take water out with a bucket or a glass bottle.
message.recompile.compost_full: The compost heap is full - harvest some fertilizer first.
message.recompile.dimension_locked: That way is sealed for now.
message.recompile.multiblock_missing_par: You're missing parts to assemble this.
message.recompile.multiblock_no_room: Not enough clear space to assemble - clear the footprint and place again.
message.recompile.needs_tool: You need a %s to open this
book.recompile.guide.name: The Salvager's Manual
book.recompile.guide.tooltip: A field guide to a world made of garbage.
book.recompile.guide.getting_started.the:
This is a world built from garbage. There are no ores, no trees, no animals, and no caves worth the trip. The surface is coarse dirt from edge to edge, and everything you need is buried in the mounds of trash on top of it.

\
\
Materials do not come from mining. They come from picking through garbage. The early game is learning how.

The one thing you must get right at the start: when you create the world, open the More tab and set the World Type to Garbage World. A normal world ignores the preset and drops you in vanilla terrain, which is the most common reason people think the mod is not working.

\
\
The garbage biome has no mob spawns by design. Nothing hunts you here, and nothing gives you meat.
book.recompile.guide.getting_started.pic:
A Block of Garbage falls like gravel, so mind what is above you. You do not have to dig one up to use it: right-click it where it stands with an empty hand and you pull one item out. Right-click again for the next.

\
\
Each block only has so much in it. After a handful of pulls it crumbles and is gone. What you get is random, weighted toward common scrap.

Trash Bags and Compacted Bales are richer streams than a plain garbage block, with their own drop tables. Some pulls want a tool in hand rather than a bare hand. If a block will not give anything up, check what it expects (Jade shows the hint).
book.recompile.guide.getting_started.mat:
Nine base materials carry the whole early game:

\
\
Junk - the filler; the bulk sink and a crafting stand-in.\
Scrap Metal - the metal vocabulary.\
Rebar - structural; a crafting spine.\
Plastic Scrap - plastics and panels.\
Glass Shards - glass and cullet.\
Fiber Scrap - cloth and padding.\
Organic Muck - compost feed.\
E-Scrap - the rare electronic bits.\
Tin Can - food (see Survival & Shelter).

\
\
You will read these names on every recipe. JEI shows which block or tool each one feeds.
book.recompile.guide.getting_started.sea:
The Nether is open. Build a frame, light it, and it works - go for what is down there and come back.

\
\
The End is still sealed and its portals will not form. That door opens in a later version, when the themed build is ready.
book.recompile.guide.tools.salvage.name: Salvage Tools
book.recompile.guide.tools.salvage.intro:
The tools here are not the wood-to-stone-to-iron ladder. They are salvage tools, crafted from the base materials, and each opens something specific:

\
\
Prybar - pries open Bulky Waste.\
Scrap Knife - cuts open Tin Cans and cuts down a Mattress at the workbench.\
Junk Shovel - digs garbage blocks and rubble out of the ground. Without one they will not come up at all, though you can still pick through them where they stand.

\
\
The right tool is often the difference between a block giving something up and giving nothing.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.crafti:
There is no wood, so there is no vanilla crafting table. You craft at the Scrap Crafting Table, and it is one of the first things you build.

\
\
It does one thing the vanilla table cannot: it reaches into the Scrap Network. Stand it against your Scrap Bins and Barrel and it crafts straight from what they hold, so you do not have to pull materials into the grid by hand first.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.sortin:
The Tarp sifts garbage without picking through it by hand. Right-click it holding a Block of Garbage, Trash Bag, Compacted Bale, Stone Rubble, Mechanical Waste, and from the Nether, Techno-Organic Waste or Slag Rubble, or from the radioactive dump, Mill Tailings or a Waste Drum. It takes one block per press, so hold right-click to keep it going.

\
\
It has no screen and stores nothing. It is a faster hand, not a machine, so stand over a place you do not mind covering in loose items, or feed it next to a Scrap Barrel.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.workbe:
The Workbench tears salvage back into materials. It has a slot for a Scrap Knife and a slot for a Prybar and holds both at once; right-click with a tool to rack it. Each teardown names the tool it needs, so rack both and nothing will turn you away. Then hold right-click on the workbench with an item to break it down.

\
\
The racked tool wears down as it works. When it breaks, anything that needed it stops coming apart until you rack another; a teardown that names no tool carries on regardless.

\
\
Some things also teach you something as they come apart, and you get an Idea Fragment along with the materials. If a Filing Cabinet is connected to the bench the fragment goes straight into it. See Blueprints.

\
\
Jade shows the racked tool, its durability, and whether what you are holding has any salvage value.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.scrap_: Every vanilla container needs wood, and there is none, so storage is its own tier. The Scrap Barrel is the general one: it opens the normal chest screen and holds a chest's worth of anything.

A Scrap Bin binds to a single item type. The first thing you file into an empty bin sets it, and after that the bin only takes that item.

\
\
Line up a wall of bins to sort one material each, then let the Scrap Network keep them filled.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.burn_b: A furnace you feed by hand

The Burn Barrel is the world's first smelter. It opens the normal furnace screen, but it is not a general furnace: it takes refuse and food and refuses everything else. Scrap Metal, kelp and anything edible will burn. Metal will not, beyond that scrap.

\
\
It takes no automation either. Hoppers and pipes cannot push into or pull out of it, so you load and unload it by hand.

\
\
It burns Oily Rag and the other salvage fuels, and lights up while it is running. The Cupola Furnace out in the demolition yard is the one that handles metal.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.scrap_:
Place the station blocks touching, sharing a face, and they form one cluster: the Scrap Crafting Table, Scrap Bins, the Scrap Barrel, the Sorting Tarp, the Teardown Workbench, the Burn Barrel, the Cupola Furnace, the Slag Furnace, the Sintering Kiln, the Dented Filing Cabinet, the Separator, the Trommel and the Pulverizer. Any face of an assembled machine counts, not just its core.

\
\
Items routed into the cluster find their own way: a bound bin that matches takes it first, otherwise the Barrel. Two actions will also set an empty bin to whatever lands in it - filing your whole haul by shift-right-clicking the Tarp, and putting a stack down inside the Scrap Crafting Table. Sifting, teardown and smelting never will, so a machine's output cannot bind a bin behind your back. No pipes, no hoppers, no screen; just put the blocks next to each other.
Blocks that route to each other
book.recompile.guide.survival.food.name: Feeding Yourself
book.recompile.guide.survival.food.intro:
The garbage biome spawns nothing, so hunting is not on the menu. Food comes from two places.

\
\
Tin Cans turn up in the pull streams. You cannot eat a sealed can; cut it open with a Scrap Knife first, then eat what is inside.

\
\
Dump Mushrooms grow on mycelium in the dump. Forage them, and replant them like vanilla mushrooms to keep a renewable patch.
book.recompile.guide.survival.food.mushr: A Dump Mushroom is a placeable item. Put it back down on mycelium and it grows again, so a foraged patch is a food source you can farm rather than strip. Fertilizer on mycelium (see Reclamation) grows more.
book.recompile.guide.survival.lighting.i:
No coal on the surface and no sticks means no vanilla torch on the normal path. Light comes from the Scrap Torch, made with an Oily Rag as the fuel.

\
\
One torch item places on the floor or on a wall, whichever surface you click.
book.recompile.guide.survival.water.name: The Rain Collector
book.recompile.guide.survival.water.intr:
There are no rivers or springs, so rain is the only fresh water. The Rain Collector catches it.

\
\
Place the collector with a Rain Collector Funnel (a Machine Frame wrapped in Plastic Scrap) and leave it under open sky; it fills when it rains. Draw water out with a bucket or a glass bottle. If you break the collector, the water it is holding comes with it and is there again when you replace it.
book.recompile.guide.survival.building.i:
Once you are drowning in scrap, the building blocks are the sink. Each material family presses into a full block plus a slab, stairs, and wall (glass adds a pane):

\
\
Pressed Junk - the everyday grey block.\
Scrap Plating - metal.\
Corrugated Metal - ribbed metal.\
Plastic Panel - plastics.\
Cullet Glass - remelted glass shards, with a pane.

\
\
These are craft targets, not drops. They turn a materials surplus into a base.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.machine:
The reclamation machines are multiblocks: a core block plus a set of parts stacked around it in a fixed shape. There are two ways to build one.

\
\
Place the core with all the parts in your inventory and it assembles itself, consuming the parts. A grey and red preview shows the footprint before you commit, so you can see if it fits. Or place the core and stack the parts by hand in the right spots.

\
\
A machine only works once it is fully formed. Break any block of it and the whole thing comes apart, dropping its parts.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.encroac:
Bringing the world back is not a one-time act. The dump takes green ground back.

\
\
Grass on the border of healed and unhealed ground reverts to coarse dirt over time. Plants you scatter are torn out first, before the grass under them, so a planted edge buys the grass a little longer. Logs and leaves make ground permanent.

\
\
Only the green is contested; it never eats down to bare rock. The sweep only runs near players, so a base does not rot while you are away.
Reclaimed ground rots at the edges

Farmland is defended by water, not by grass. A watered plot holds against the dump. A plot that dries out is taken back with the soil under it. A crop on lost farmland pops off as an item, so you lose the plot and the growth but keep the seed. Keep your fields irrigated.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.grass_s:
Rung one of reclamation. The Grass Spreader waters the ground around it and turns coarse dirt straight to grass, one block at a time. It also keeps nearby farmland wet, like a water source.

\
\
It sits idle until the whole tower is up. After that it runs forever on its own - there is nothing to fill and nothing to feed it.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.vegetat:
Rung two. Right-click reclaimed grass with Fertilizer to scatter weeds and wildflowers across it - the pioneer plants that come back to disturbed ground.

\
\
Fertilizer does nothing on the raw dump, so heal the ground with a Grass Spreader first. The plants it grows are the first thing the dump strips at a contested edge, so a fertilized border holds a little longer while you push out.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.farming:
Rung three. A hoe will not till the dump. You craft farmland instead: Fertilizer plus dirt (or coarse dirt and more fertilizer). The compost recipe is the only way to a plot.

\
\
Seeds are not bought or found loose; they come from compost. The Heap now and then drops an Unknown Seedling that becomes a random one of the six crops when you plant it.

\
\
Keep plots watered with a Grass Spreader or rain. A dry plot dries out and the dump takes it.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.compost:
Fertilizer comes from the Compost Heap, a two-by-two-by-two cage of seven Machine Frames around a core (it assembles itself if you are carrying them).

\
\
Feed it any compostable - Organic Muck, Fiber Scrap, or plant matter like leaves, grass, saplings, crops and seeds. Every few items form a layer, each layer ripens on its own timer, and a ripe layer is right-clicked out for one Fertilizer. It never has to be full to give something back.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.sapling:
Saplings are stripped from every drop, so you will never find one. This is on purpose. A found sapling could grow a tree on raw coarse dirt and permanently anchor ground you have not actually reclaimed.

\
\
The Tree Nursery is the only thing that makes one, and it is the next entry over. Until you build it, reclamation tops out at grass, plants and crops.
You will not find a sapling
book.recompile.guide.collectibles.puzzle:
The Puzzle Cube is the first collectible, and the only one you assemble. Its nine pieces turn up rarely in the pull streams; when you have all nine, fill the crafting grid with them to build the cube.

\
\
The cube is a real block you place and display. Craft it with itself to scramble it, and again to solve it.
book.recompile.guide.collectibles.curios:
Some curios are found whole rather than assembled - an avocado, a wrapped present, a gold coin, a toy car. They are rare, a few times rarer than a single Puzzle Cube piece, and they turn up intact in the same pick-through streams.

\
\
There is nothing to craft; you either find one or you do not. Set it on a pedestal and keep looking for the rest.
book.recompile.guide.collectibles.pedest:
The Display Pedestal holds one item and floats it, slowly turning, above the cap. It takes any item, so a collectible is only the obvious thing to set on it. It is a display, not storage: no hopper feeds it, and it drops what it holds when you take it or break it.

\
\
Because it shows the item's real model, a placed block like the Puzzle Cube stands up there as a true 3D object.
book.recompile.guide.reference.toggles.i:
Most of the mod's behavior is config-gated. Defaults are the intended game, but a pack or a player can change them.

\
\
The switches worth knowing: garbage-block gravity, the encroachment sweep, the dimension lockout, and the reclamation numbers. This entry is the orientation; the config file itself is where the values live and is commented per option.
book.recompile.guide.reference.viewers.i:
Two viewer mods, if you run them, surface the non-vanilla mechanics in-game.

\
\
JEI adds Sorting, Cutting, and Prying categories, so you can look up what a garbage block, a knife, or a prybar yields, and it shows the Scrap Crafting Table as the station.

\
\
Jade shows block hints on look: which tool a block wants, how far a Grass Spreader reaches, how many layers a Compost Heap has, and the sort progress on a garbage block.
The mechanics that are not recipes
message.recompile.mattress_spawn_set: Respawn point set. Sleeping here will use up the mattress.
message.recompile.torch_no_fuel: The torch is empty - right-click with an Oily Rag to charge it
message.recompile.torch_needs_rag: You need an Oily Rag to charge the torch
tooltip.recompile.torch_charge_hint: Right-click with an Oily Rag to charge
message.recompile.torch_too_full: The torch is too full to take a whole rag
book.recompile.guide.demolition.slag_fur:
Slag is what a furnace could not use. Melt it again, hot enough and long enough, and it stops being a lump of grit: the whole thing goes liquid and freezes as a black glass. That is obsidian, and it is the only way you will ever hold any.

\
\
Build the furnace out of a Cupola and eight Steel Offcuts. The Cupola is the machine that makes the slag, so you cannot own this one without having owned that one, which is the order it wants anyway. Steel and not copper for the shell: copper melts well below the temperature this runs at.

\
\
One slag to a block, and it is a slow burn - twice as long as a normal smelt. The cost is upstream: the Cupola only rakes one lump every eighth smelt. Nothing else in the game does this. No furnace, no blast furnace, no campfire. The operation belongs to this machine alone, which is what makes the black glass worth the walk out to the yard.

\
\
It routes like the rest of them. Put a Scrap Bin or the Barrel against it and the glass files itself away.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.slag.int:
Melt scrap and you do not only get metal. Everything in it that is not metal - grit, rust, the dirt that came in with it - floats to the top and cools into a hard grey lump.

\
\
The Cupola rakes one off every eighth smelt into a second output slot beside the metal. You did not ask for it and you cannot stop it. Let that slot fill and the furnace keeps working - it simply remembers what it owes you and hands it over once there is room.

\
\
Two machines will take it. A Separator divides it into concrete powder, and finds the metal droplets left in it. A Pulverizer grinds it into Fertilizer, which is not a trick - ground slag really was sold as fertiliser for a hundred years. And a Slag Furnace melts it all the way down into obsidian.
jei.recompile.info.burn_barrel: Burns refuse only: food, and scrap metal for copper. It will not smelt ore, sand, stone or logs - a drum fire does not get hot enough. Upgrade it into a Cupola Furnace to smelt everything else.
jei.recompile.info.cupola_furnace: A coke-fired shaft furnace for remelting scrap. It melts metal and nothing else: scrap into copper, steel offcuts into iron, rebar into nuggets. Food and refuse stay with the Burn Barrel. Unlike the barrel it takes hoppers.
jei.recompile.info.cutting_torch: Right-click holding the torch to feed it an Oily Rag. Each rag is worth 8 cuts and it holds 64. Cutting steel spends one charge; with an empty torch the cut is refused.
jei.recompile.info.steel_offcut: Cut off a Steel I-Beam with a Cutting Torch. Remelt it into iron in a Cupola Furnace - the Burn Barrel will not take it.
jei.recompile.info.burner_generator: Burns refuse for power. Right-click to open its fuel buffer and load anything a furnace would burn - an Oily Rag will do. It takes one item at a time, so a stack lasts, and hoppers or pipes can keep it stocked. Energy goes straight into whatever it is touching; hover it to see how much it is holding.
jei.recompile.info.hydroponics_bay:
Built only from the Hydroponics Bay blueprint, at the Scrap Crafting Table. Tear down Broken Hydroponics Bays to learn it - six Idea Fragments make the blueprint.

Grows plants without soil, on water and power together. Right-click with a water bucket to fill its tank; the two gauges are water on the left and power on the right, and it needs both to run. The plant you put in stays there and keeps growing until you take it back out, so it takes one and only one. Sugar cane, bamboo, cactus and sweet berries have no other source in this world.
jei.recompile.info.unknown_seedling: Plant it and find out what it was. In a Hydroponics Bay it grows into one random plant from the list, which you can then put back in to grow that plant for good.
jei.recompile.info.solar_panel: Generates power from daylight, and needs an open sky - a block overhead stops it. Output falls off at dusk and in bad weather rather than cutting out. It also still works as a machine part: a panel inside a Grass Spreader or Tree Nursery generates as well, and those machines do not need power to run.
tooltip.recompile.generator_buffer_full: Buffer full - nothing is drawing power
jei.recompile.info.raw_roach: Something lives in the garbage. Picking through a Block of Garbage occasionally disturbs a roach instead of turning up anything useful - one at a time, and only from household garbage. Kill it yourself and it leaves meat; anything else that kills it leaves nothing. Cook it in the Burn Barrel.
book.recompile.guide.survival.roaches.in:
Sooner or later a Block of Garbage gives up a roach instead of a material. One roach, from household garbage only, and it costs you that pull.

\
\
Kill it yourself for Raw Roach - if something else kills it, there is nothing left. Cook it in the Burn Barrel. It is not good food, but it is food you can get on the first day, which nothing else out here is.

painting.recompile.pearl_earring.author: Johannes Vermeer
painting.recompile.la_grande_jatte.title: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
book.recompile.guide.demolition.the_yard:
Biomes here are placed by how far you are from where you spawned, not by climate. Within 512 blocks of the origin the ground is always household sprawl, so a first base cannot be stranded in something harder.

\
\
Past 512 blocks the demolition yard starts appearing, and the further out you go the less household ground there is between the patches. Travel is the gate: everything in the next three entries exists only out there.

\
\
The yard is the only source of stone, concrete and steel. Nothing in the household sprawl substitutes for any of them.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.concrete:
Reinforced Concrete needs a Sledgehammer. No other tool drops anything from it, and the Sledgehammer mines nothing else.

\
\
Breaking a block gives gravel, sand or concrete powder, and about a third of the time a Rebar as well. Some of the sand comes out red. That is rust: the aggregate nearest the steel has been staining for as long as this place has been standing, and red sand is iron-stained sand wherever you find it. Nothing else you can dig up here is red, and the whole red sandstone family comes off it.

\
\
Sand is glass, and several later machines are built out of glass, so a Sledgehammer and a stretch of concrete are what stand between you and the automation tier. The fine pale silt in a sewer brushes down into sand too, if you would rather dig than smash - though the coarse grey silt is gravel, so look at what you are brushing.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.steel.in:
Steel I-Beams stand in stacks out in the yard and in the frames of ruined buildings. They are the bulk metal of this world.

\
\
A beam only comes apart under a Cutting Torch. Right-click holding the torch to feed it an Oily Rag: one rag is worth eight cuts and the torch holds sixty-four. Each cut spends a charge, and an empty torch refuses to cut.

\
\
What you get is Steel Offcuts. They are not iron yet.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.iron.int:
Steel Offcuts and Rebar only become iron in a Cupola Furnace. It is a shaft furnace for remelting metal: scrap into copper, offcuts into iron ingots, rebar into nuggets.

\
\
No other furnace will do it. The Burn Barrel refuses metal outright, and these are blast recipes, which an ordinary furnace cannot run at all. That is the whole of the iron gate: build the Cupola or stay on copper.

\
\
The Cupola does not cook food, deliberately. Keep the Burn Barrel for that. Unlike the barrel, the Cupola accepts hoppers.
book.recompile.guide.power.energy.name: Power
Generators push energy directly into whatever block they are touching. There is no cable and no network to build, so a machine is powered by being placed against a generator.

\
\
Every machine holds its own buffer, which is why one keeps running for a while after its generator stops. Hover a generator or a machine with Jade to see how much it is holding.

\
\
It is standard Forge Energy, so anything from another mod that speaks it will work here.
book.recompile.guide.power.generators.in:
The Solar Panel needs open sky. A block overhead stops it, and its output falls off at dusk and in bad weather rather than cutting out. It is slow and it is free.

\
\
The Burner Generator burns refuse for power, far faster. Right-click it and load anything a furnace would burn; an Oily Rag will do. It takes one item at a time, so a stack lasts, and hoppers or pipes can keep it stocked.

\
\
A Solar Panel also still counts as a machine part. One built into a Grass Spreader or a Tree Nursery generates as well, and neither of those machines needs power to run.
book.recompile.guide.power.hydroponics.i:
The bay cannot be crafted until you have worked out how. Pry Broken Hydroponics Bays out of Bulky Waste and tear them down at the Teardown Workbench until you have the blueprint; see Blueprints.

\
\
The recipe also needs a Bulb, which turns up in ordinary household sorting. A bay built under a mound has no other light.

\
\
It runs on water and power together and stops without either. Right-click it with a water bucket to fill the tank. Water is the left gauge, power the right; hover either for the numbers.

\
\
It takes one plant and keeps it. What you put in is not consumed - it stays and keeps producing until you take it back out - so the slot holds exactly one. Seed crops go in as their seed, the same as planting them in the ground: wheat seeds in, wheat out. Potatoes and carrots are their own seed.

\
\
Of the two harvest slots, the upper one is the crop and the lower catches byproducts: seeds off wheat and beetroot, and the occasional poisonous potato. If either has nowhere to put what is coming, the bay stops rather than losing it.

\
\
Start with an Unknown Seedling. One batch turns it into a random plant, which you then plant properly. Sugar cane, bamboo, cactus, sweet berries, kelp and cocoa have no other source in this world.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.nursery:
Rung 4. The Tree Nursery grows saplings, and nothing else in this world does. Much later a wandering trader will sell you one, once you have emeralds - and emeralds mean a cured villager, which means a brewing stand, which means the Nether. That is the only other way there is, and it is a very long way from here.

\
\
Crafting it needs a Bulb, out of ordinary household sorting. A seedling started indoors has no sky over it, so the light has to come from somewhere.

\
\
It is a 2x2x1 wall of a Water Tank and two Solar Panels around the core. Fill it with a water bucket, feed it Fertilizer and an Unknown Seedling, and pick the species you want from the screen.

\
\
A sapling out of the nursery plants and grows like any other. Trees anchor reclaimed ground permanently against the encroaching dump, which is why they are gated behind a machine instead of turning up in the garbage.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.bait.in:
Rung 5. There are no animals in this world to begin with. Bait is how you get them.

\
\
Place it on grass, which means ground you have already reclaimed, then walk away: nothing will come while you are standing next to it. Space your baits out rather than clustering them.

\
\
There are three diets - herbivore, carnivore, omnivore - and each decides which animals a bait can draw. The Rich grade of each brings a bonded pair instead of a single animal, which is what you want if you mean to breed them.
book.recompile.guide.collectibles.painti:
Six real paintings turn up in Bulky Waste, rarely. Each is a specific work, with its title and painter written on the item rather than a random canvas.

\
\
A recovered painting keeps its identity. Place it and you get that painting; break it and what you pick up is still that painting. That is the difference between these and a vanilla one.

\
\
They are sized to their originals, so a portrait hangs as a portrait. Check the wall you have before you place one.
book.recompile.guide.survival.sleeping.i:
A vanilla bed needs planks, and there is no wood here for a long time. The mattress out of Bulky Waste is not a stand-in for a bed. It is the bed.

\
\
Put it down and sleep on it as you would any bed. It sets your respawn point the same way.

\
\
You cannot craft one. The dump is where beds come from.
book.recompile.guide.survival.water.sour:
Two water sources placed near each other do not fill in a third. The infinite water trick does not work here.

\
\
Every bucket you pour out is a bucket gone. That is why the Rain Collector is still worth having after you can make buckets, and why a machine that drinks water needs a supply rather than one trip to a pond.
tooltip.recompile.blueprint_blank: Blank - it never said what it was for
tooltip.recompile.fragment_blank: An idea about nothing in particular
book.recompile.guide.workstations.bluepr: Working out how it was made

Some things cannot be crafted at all until you have worked out how they were made.

\
\
Tear something apart at the Teardown Workbench and you come away with an Idea Fragment as well as the materials, every time. Enough fragments about the same thing craft into a Blueprint, and once you hold that Blueprint the workbench stops handing out fragments for it.

\
\
The Blueprint is not spent. Hold it, or keep it in a Filing Cabinet, and the Scrap Crafting Table will make what it describes. A vanilla crafting table will not, ever - the recipe does not exist there.

\
\
Six things are locked this way, and each is taught by the wreck of itself. A dirty mattress teaches the Clean Mattress, which is the only route to a bed. A Broken Hydroponics Bay teaches the working one. A Washing Machine teaches the Pump, a Broken Fan the Motor, and a Light Fixture the Bulb. The sixth is not in this world at all: a Worn Forging Die, found deep in the Nether, teaches the pattern for upgrading netherite.

\
\
The three components are the odd ones. You can still pull a Pump, a Motor or a Bulb straight out of the thing it came in, so their blueprints are not the only way to get one - they are what you fall back on when you have run out of things to take apart. Four teardowns pay for each.

Pry one out of Bulky Waste. It takes blueprints and the fragments that become them, and nothing else.

\
\
Tip fragments in and the cabinet does the filing: once there are enough for a blueprint it assembles one itself. Any fragments left over for a blueprint it already holds are thrown away, because a second copy of something you know is worth nothing.

\
\
Put the cabinet against the Scrap Crafting Table, the way you would a Scrap Bin, and the table can use every blueprint filed in it. Across the room does not work: it has to be touching the table or touching something that is.

\
\
Until you find one, carrying the sheet works just as well.
jei.recompile.info.blueprint: A recipe recovered from something you tore apart. It is never used up: hold it, or keep it in a Filing Cabinet touching the Scrap Crafting Table, and that table can build what it describes. No other crafting table can.
jei.recompile.info.idea_fragment: Part of working out how something was made. Tearing down the right object at the Teardown Workbench yields one every time. Four fragments about the same thing craft into that Blueprint; fragments about different things do not combine. Once you own the Blueprint - carried or filed in a cabinet next to the bench - it stops giving you fragments for it.
jei.recompile.info.filing_cabinet: Found in Bulky Waste. Takes blueprints and Idea Fragments and nothing else. Drop fragments in and it assembles them into the blueprint on its own; spare fragments for a blueprint it already holds are discarded. Place it touching the Scrap Crafting Table and everything filed inside becomes usable there without carrying any of it.
jei.recompile.info.clean_mattress: Made only from the Clean Mattress blueprint, at the Scrap Crafting Table. Three wool and three string. Dye it any colour at an ordinary crafting table, then a mattress plus three planks makes the bed of that colour - it is the only way to make a bed in this world, since wool alone no longer does it.
jei.recompile.info.broken_hydroponics_ba: Pried out of Bulky Waste. It will never work again, but it is the only thing that shows you how one was built: tear it down at the Teardown Workbench for its parts, its scrap and an Idea Fragment. Six fragments make the Hydroponics Bay blueprint.
book.recompile.guide.survival.leachate.i:
The dark pools out in the sprawl are rain that has drained down through the refuse. It looks like water and it is not.

\
\
A Rain Collector will not take it, and a crop planted beside a pool will not be watered by it. Stand in one and you will be hungry a few seconds later. It does no damage on contact.

\
\
You can drown in it, exactly as you would in water. The pools out here are one block deep, so walking through one is safe and crawling or swimming through one is not.

\
\
You can carry it in a bucket. There is nothing yet that wants it.
jei.recompile.info.leachate_bucket: Rain that has drained down through the refuse and pooled at a low point. Pools of it sit out in the household sprawl. It does not water crops and it is not a source of clean water: it is what the dump does to rain, not a resource.
jei.recompile.info.printer: Pried out of Bulky Waste. Tear it down at the Teardown Workbench with a Prybar for paper, an ink sac, plastic and scrap, and often a lapis lazuli. Toner comes out too: fourteen dye colours are possible, cyan, magenta and yellow most often. Blue and black are not among them because the lapis and the ink sac already grind into those dyes.
jei.recompile.transfer_missing: Not in your inventory or any connected storage
container.recompile.needs_blueprint: No blueprint in your inventory or attached storage
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.compost: The core is the bottom north-west corner, not the middle. The cage builds up, east and south of it.
book.recompile.guide.reclamation.nursery: The wall has a facing. It builds across whichever way you are looking when you place the core.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.mechanic:
Heaps of dead machinery turn up in the demolition yard, beside the rubble. Pick through one bare-hand, the same way you pick through garbage.

\
\
What comes out is industrial scrap: Spent Abrasive, Magnet Scrap and Quartz Grit, along with the usual metal and cable. Nothing valuable ever falls out of the pile itself. Diamond, redstone and amethyst are separated out of that scrap afterwards, in a Separator.

\
\
The three are not equally common. Quartz Grit is everywhere, Spent Abrasive turns up often enough, and Magnet Scrap is the one you will be short of.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.separato:
The Separator runs on power. Drop scrap into the grinding bay on top and the results leave through the chute at the bottom. It holds nine kinds at once and works through them in order.

\
\
One scrap makes one raw material: Magnet Scrap for redstone, Spent Abrasive for diamond, Quartz Grit for amethyst. You get ordinary metal or glass back alongside it, because a separator splits a feed into all of its parts. The rarity is in the pile, not in the machine, so anything you find is worth putting through.

Four Steel I-Beams make the 2x2 grinding bay. Six Machine Frames and one Motor make the rest: the column beside the bay, the back row, and the chute next to the core.

\
\
The Motor sits in the middle of the back row. It is the drive, it is salvaged out of Mechanical Waste, and no quantity of scrap substitutes for one. Take the machine apart and you get it back.
A trommel is a long perforated drum, turning slowly, with the small material falling through the screen and the oversize riding out the end. It is the first machine in a real sorting plant, and it is the one here that takes over from the Sorting Tarp.

\
\
Feed it a Block of Garbage, Trash Bag, Compacted Bale, Stone Rubble, Mechanical Waste, and from the Nether, Techno-Organic Waste or Slag Rubble, or from the radioactive dump, Mill Tailings or a Waste Drum and it sorts them.

\
\
It yields exactly what the tarp yields. A Block of Garbage gives the same pulls either way, and at one block every two seconds a determined player at a tarp is faster. The machine does not pay you more; it pays you while you are somewhere else. Build a second one rather than waiting on the first.

\
\
It runs on power, and it does nothing at all without it.

Four Steel I-Beams make the drum, in a row along the top. The core, one Motor and two Machine Frames make the stand underneath it, and the far end of the stand becomes the discharge.

\
\
The Motor is the drive. A drum that turns needs something turning it, and no quantity of scrap substitutes for one: it comes out of Mechanical Waste. Take the machine apart and you get it back.

Nothing can push into a Trommel. There is no hopper you can point at it and no pipe that will connect. It reaches out and takes instead, and there are two ways to let it.

\
\
Drop material anywhere along the top of the drum and it will swallow it. That is the quick way, and it is what you do while you are standing there.

\
\
Or stand a chest, a barrel or a hopper on the drum and the machine will empty it, a little at a time. That is the way that runs without you: fill the chest however you like, and the Trommel drains it.

\
\
What comes out goes into any Scrap Bins wired to the machine, then out of the open end of the drum - into whatever you park there, or thrown clear if there is nothing.

\
\
It only swallows what it can sort. Anything else stays lying where you dropped it.
Bulky Waste is the big buried item, not a pick-through block. Right-click it with a Prybar and it opens in one action: it drops a single find and breaks. Without a Prybar it tells you what it needs, and mining it by hand gives nothing.

Most opens give one of the six ordinary finds on the right. About one in ten gives something from the better pool instead, and there is a small chance of a recovered painting.

\
\
A find is a real item. You can carry it home and place it, and most of them tear down at the Teardown Workbench into parts nothing else provides.
book.recompile.guide.bulky_waste.mattres:
Sleep on it once and it is destroyed when you get up. It is a way to survive a night, not a place to live.

\
\
The other use is better. Tear it down at the Teardown Workbench with a Scrap Knife for string, fiber and scrap, and every teardown also gives you an idea toward the Clean Mattress. Four of those make the blueprint, and a Clean Mattress plus three planks is the only bed in this world.
book.recompile.guide.bulky_waste.washing:
The dependable source of a Pump, and the Pump is what a Grass Spreader is built from. A Dead Fridge gives one sometimes, but only sometimes.

\
\
Tear it down at the Workbench with a Prybar: one Pump, scrap metal and plastic. Every teardown also teaches you something about the pump itself, and four of them make its Blueprint. After that you can build Pumps from copper and scrap at the Scrap Crafting Table without finding another machine.

\
\
It also places as a block if you would rather keep it standing.
book.recompile.guide.bulky_waste.printer:
Tear it down at the Workbench with a Prybar for paper, an ink sac, plastic and scrap, and about half the time a lapis lazuli.

\
\
Toner is the rest of it. Fourteen dye colours can come out, cyan, magenta and yellow several times more often than the rest. Blue and black are not among them because the teardown already handed you both: lapis grinds into blue dye, an ink sac into black.

\
\
White is the one worth the find. Its only other route is bone meal, which means either skeleton bones from the demolition yard or a composter you cannot build without wood. Gray, pink and light blue are each white plus something, and magenta needs pink.
Two blocks tall, and the only find that is. Pry it open like any other Bulky Waste; it comes up whole.

\
\
Tearing one down does not work like the rest. You get eight pieces of scrap split between metal, plastic and electronics, one thing that was left in the freezer, and one component out of a Motor, a Pump and a Bulb.

\
\
You do not choose which component. Whichever one comes out is the one you learn about, so a Blueprint takes four fridges that happened to give you the same part.

Snow most of the time, ice the rest of it. This is the only ice or snow in the world: nothing here snows, and there is no water standing still long enough to freeze.

\
\
It is ordinary ice, which in a world with no other water is worth thinking about.
book.recompile.guide.bulky_waste.filing_:
Takes blueprints and Idea Fragments and nothing else. Drop loose fragments in and it assembles them into sheets on its own; spares toward a sheet it already holds are thrown away.

\
\
Place it touching a Scrap Crafting Table and everything filed inside counts as being in your inventory while you craft there.
book.recompile.guide.bulky_waste.broken_: It will never work again. Tearing it down at the Workbench is the only way to learn how one was built: parts, scrap and an Idea Fragment every time. Six fragments make the Hydroponics Bay blueprint.
book.recompile.guide.bulky_waste.windfal:
About one find in ten comes from a second, rarer pool: a bookshelf, a jukebox, a bell, or a spyglass.

\
\
A bell has no crafting recipe in any version of the game. A jukebox needs a diamond and a spyglass needs an amethyst shard, and both of those are behind the demolition yard and the Separator. Finding one skips a long way ahead.
message.recompile.needs_dig_tool: You need a %s to dig this out - or right-click to sort it by hand
book.recompile.guide.getting_started.pic: Sorting a pile is bare-hand work and always will be. Carrying one home is a different job and wants a tool: a shovel for garbage and rubble, a pickaxe for mechanical waste, a scrap knife for a bale. Swing without one and the pile stays where it is and tells you what it wants, so nothing is lost while you learn it. Trash bags come up by hand.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.sewers.i:
There are brick tunnels under the demolition yard. You find them from above: a square of pale concrete set flush in the ground, with a rusted steel plate in the middle of it.

\
\
The plate comes up with a Prybar and nothing else. Bare hands will tell you so. Under it is a ladder, and the ladder goes a long way down.

Bring a light and something to fight with. The corridors run with leachate. It will leave you hungry, and you can drown in it, so use the dry brick either side of the channel.

\
\
Roaches live down here and nowhere else, and slimes are far commoner down here than up on the yard. So do drowned, around whatever is spawning them. Turtles and frogs are down there too, and there are only ever as many as you find - nothing replaces them.

\
\
Cobwebs come off with shears. The barrels are the reason to have come.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.sewers.s:
Some of the gravel and sand down here is not quite either. It gathers in the corners of the runs and it covers the floor of the sump, and a shovel takes it apart without giving you anything back.

\
\
Use a brush. Most of it is silt and you get nothing, which is what silt is. Now and then something that went down a drain a long time ago comes back out of it.

\
\
A brush is a feather, a stick and a copper ingot, so you want chickens before you want this.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.sewers.b:
Every channel runs downhill, and they all run to the same room. The sump is the low point: standing leachate deep enough to go over your head, no lamp, and whatever accumulated in it.

\
\
A walkway crosses the entrance so you see the water before you are in it. Past that there is only the pool.

\
\
Something washed down here and settled in the gravel. It is the one thing a sewer gives that nothing else in the world will.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.pulveriz:
A mill, not a shredder. The Separator tears a thing into its parts; this one only makes it finer. If what comes out is the same material in smaller pieces, it belongs here.

\
\
Inside is a rotor swinging hammers in a sealed steel box. You cannot see in, and you would not want to.

\
\
Feed it bone and you get bone meal, four from a bone and nine from a block. That is worth the power because you are not standing at a crafting grid to do it.

\
\
It runs on power and does nothing at all without it.

A cube, two blocks on every side. The core sits in a bottom corner with the Motor beside it, two Machine Frames finish the base, and four Steel I-Beams make the top half where the rotor lives.

\
\
The Motor is the drive. No amount of scrap makes one; you find it in Mechanical Waste. Take the machine apart and you get it back.

Nothing can push into a Pulverizer. It reaches out and takes instead.

\
\
Drop material on the roof and it swallows it, or stand a chest, barrel or hopper up there and the machine empties it a little at a time. That is the way that runs without you.

\
\
Powder leaves by the front, into any Scrap Bins wired to the machine first, then into whatever you park there, then on the floor.

\
\
It only swallows what it has a recipe for. Anything else stays lying on top.
jade.recompile.pulverizer_feed: Feed: drop material on the hatch, or set a container on it
jei.recompile.cupola.slag_any: Counted, not rolled - and any smelt counts
jade.recompile.separator_feed: Feed: drop scrap in the bay, or set a container on it
book.recompile.guide.demolition.separato:
Nothing can push into a Separator. It reaches out and takes instead.

\
\
Drop scrap into the bay on top and it swallows it, or stand a chest, barrel or hopper on the bay and the machine empties it a little at a time. That is the way that runs without you.

\
\
What comes out goes into any Scrap Bins wired to the machine first, then into whatever you park at the chute, then on the floor.

\
\
It only swallows what it has a recipe for - Blocks of Garbage and the like go to a Trommel now, not here. Anything else stays lying in the bay.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.gold.int: There is gold in the boards

A tonne of circuit boards carries more gold than a tonne of ore - by a wide margin. It is the reason anyone bothers taking electronics apart, and it is the reason this world has no gold in the ground and plenty in the rubbish.

\
\
You cannot get at it by burning boards whole. The metal is locked in resin and glass, and a furnace will not free it. It has to be ground first.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.gold.rou:
Grind E-Scrap in a Pulverizer and it comes out as Circuit Powder. That is the stage that frees the metal; nothing before it will do.

\
\
Blast the powder in a Cupola Furnace and you get a gold nugget. A nugget, not an ingot - you are recovering traces out of rubbish, not mining a seam.

\
\
An ordinary furnace will not do this, and neither will the Burn Barrel - it takes a blast. The Cupola is the first thing in this world that can, and until you have iron it is the only one.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.clay.int:
There is no clay in the ground here. There are broken pots, and pots were clay once - but firing is a one-way door. Grind a sherd and add water and you get wet grit, not clay.

\
\
What crushed pottery actually is is grog, and potters really do mix it back into new clay. It controls shrinkage and stops things cracking in the kiln. What it will not do is hold together, because that is the opposite of its job.

\
\
So the stickiness has to come from somewhere else. It comes from the cat litter.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.clay.rou:
Crush a pottery sherd in a Pulverizer for one Grog. Any sherd will do - the picture does not survive being ground.

\
\
Mix three Grog with one Kitty Litter in a crafting grid for a Dry Clay Body. Blending dry before adding water is how it is really done.

\
\
Then right-click the Dry Clay Body on a water cauldron. That is your clay, and it costs a level of water.

\
\
Kitty litter turns up in the dump long before you can use it. Keep it - it is bentonite, and it is the only thing in this world that will make a clay body stick together.
book.recompile.guide.depths.getting_ther:
You will not mine obsidian. None of it is in the ground anywhere, in either world, and a few blocks in a fortress chest is a lucky find rather than a supply.

\
\
The route that works is the Cupola Furnace. It rakes off a lump of slag every few smelts into its second output slot - you did not ask for it and you cannot ask for it, because it is the fraction that floats off any remelt. Feed that slag to a Slag Furnace and it comes back as obsidian, a lump to a block.

\
\
So the portal is paid for upstream, in the smelting you had already done. The chapter on the demolition yard has the numbers.
book.recompile.guide.depths.the_fill.int:
There is no cavern down here, no lava sea, and no ceiling to fall from. Every column is full from the bedrock floor to the bedrock ceiling, and the only open spaces are the things buried in it.

\
\
Techno-organic waste is the fill, and it behaves the way a Block of Garbage does: right-click to pick through it and it gives up one thing at a time until it crumbles. It does not fall, which is deliberate. A dimension of falling blocks would bury you the moment you started digging.

\
\
Slag rubble is the spoil caught inside it, and that does fall. Fortresses and bastions are down here too, and everything vanilla puts in them is still there.
book.recompile.guide.depths.terrain.name: Terrain Is Rebuilt
book.recompile.guide.depths.terrain.intr:
No nether terrain generates down here. Not one block of netherrack, basalt, blackstone or soul sand is in the ground you are digging through.

\
\
Sorting slag rubble gives shards, and four shards of a kind craft the block they came from. Short of quarrying a fortress or a bastion for the stone somebody else built it out of, that is how you get any of it - which is what makes this a dimension worth mining rather than a place to walk through.

\
\
Two of the seven are worth more than the block they make. Bone meal on nylium grows fungus, and a fungus bone-mealed on its own nylium becomes a huge one. Nothing down here grows a fungus forest on its own, so those shards are the only seed for one.
book.recompile.guide.depths.scrap.name: Scrap, Not Materials
The waste gives you scrap. Your machines give you materials. It is the same rule the surface runs on: a household mound has no copper in it, it has scrap metal, and the Cupola does the rest.

\
\
Fused Circuitry goes to a Separator and comes out as quartz, with circuit powder alongside it - which is where gold starts. Phosphor Scrap goes to a Pulverizer and comes out as glowstone dust. Rendered Organics go to a Separator for nether wart, which grows on the soul sand the rubble already gave you.

\
\
Oily Swarf answers to both. Ground fine it burns, and gives blaze powder. Separated, the cutting oil comes off it as magma cream and the chips come off as scrap metal. One material, two machines, two different jobs.
book.recompile.guide.depths.coal.name: Coal, At Last
book.recompile.guide.depths.coal.intro.t:
Lignite is brown coal - a real rank of it, the one below the coal you know. Smelting a lump gives you that coal, and short of taking it off a wither skeleton there is nowhere else it comes from.

\
\
It burns on its own before you upgrade it, at about half a coal's worth. That is worth knowing, because there is nothing down here to cut for charcoal until you have grown it. Upgrading still pays: one lignite of heat is enough to smelt four more.

\
\
You will not miss much if you never bother. Charcoal already covers every recipe that takes coal, except the block you store it in.
book.recompile.guide.depths.netherite.in:
Netherite scrap comes out of the waste on its own, rarely. Gold comes off the circuit powder. So the ingots are yours. Upgrading anything with them is not, because that needs a smithing template, and the only recipe for one of those consumes a template to make it.

\
\
A Worn Forging Die is what breaks the circle. A forging die is the block a press shapes metal against, so the pattern lives in the die - which is exactly what a smithing template is.

\
\
Tear one down at the Workbench with a prybar. It gives up almost nothing, because a worn-out die has nothing left to give but its shape - and the shape is the point. Four of them and you have the pattern for good.

\
\
It is expensive on purpose. Making a template from the pattern costs more than copying one you already have, so a bastion is still the quick way in and this is the way that does not need one.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.sinterin:
Every other machine here takes something apart. The Trommel cuts a block into its drops, the Separator splits a mixture, the Pulverizer grinds things finer, the Slag Furnace melts rock to glass. The kiln is the one that puts something back together.

\
\
It fires a pressed powder until the grains fuse. Not melting - a kiln holds a heat below that and waits, which is how you make a solid out of dust without turning it into a puddle.

\
\
There are two things to fire, and either would be worth the machine on its own. Press four blaze powder into a briquette at a bench, fire the briquette, and you get a blaze rod back. That is a brewing stand, and every potion behind it, without setting foot in a fortress.

\
\
Press four gunpowder the same way and you get a breeze rod instead. Nothing in this world drops one - the breezes that carry them live in trial chambers, and there are none here - so this is the only breeze rod there is, and the only wind charges. A rod makes four of them.

\
\
The four is not arbitrary. A blaze rod breaks down into two powder, so if a rod cost any less than that you could make rods out of nothing by going round in circles. It costs four and gives back two, and that is the end of it.

\
\
A breeze rod cannot be broken down at all, so its four is doing a different job: a rod makes four wind charges, which puts one charge at one gunpowder.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.the_yard:
It is also the only place a person survives out here. There are no villages in this world, so the zombie villagers that turn up among the ordinary zombies are the only villagers there will ever be. Cure one the usual way - weakness, then a golden apple - and you have the only villager you will ever trade with.

\
\
Weakness has two routes and one of them costs nothing. Brew it, which needs a stand and so a blaze rod and so the Nether. Or stand beside the zombie villager and let a witch throw one at you: witches are out here too, at the same rarity, and a splash potion catches everything near where it lands.

\
\
The golden apple is the part that actually takes work. Eight gold ingots, and gold here is ground-up circuit boards blasted in a Cupola. The apple comes off an oak, so a Tree Nursery first - or a bastion chest, if you are down in the Nether anyway.
book.recompile.guide.depths.sculk.name: Ancient Sculk
Something down here is alive. Rare seams of dark growth run through the waste, lit from inside by a blue-green glow, and they are the only sculk in this world - there is no deep dark, and no city under one.

\
\
It gives nothing to a hand or a pick or a lesser hammer. A diamond sledgehammer will break it, and so will a netherite one; the copper and iron ones will not, however long you swing them. Break it properly and it comes apart into sculk powder.

\
\
The powder is the whole family. It packs back into sculk, spreads into veins, and builds a sensor around a piece of redstone or a shrieker around soul sand.

\
\
A catalyst costs an echo shard, and there is one of those at the bottom of each sewer. That is a hard price for a block, and it is the right one: a catalyst grows sculk wherever something dies near it, so you only ever need the one.
book.recompile.guide.demolition.radioact:
Keep going past the demolition yard and the ground turns sallow. Somebody buried the things nobody would take out here: heaps of mill tailings, steel drums with a trefoil stencilled on the side, and the ordinary household objects that were quietly radioactive all along.

\
\
Tailings take a sledgehammer, any of them. The drums take a prybar, the way bulky waste does.

\
\
You will probably find the place before you can work it. That is the shape of the trip: the walk is easy and the tool is not.

The stained ground under the heaps does not come back. Grass will not spread onto it and the spreader will not take it, so a patch you find stained stays stained. Everything around it behaves as it does at home.

\
\
The heaps do not come back either. Strip a dump and it is stripped - there is no mound memory out here the way there is under the sprawl. There are other dumps.
book.recompile.guide.workstations.sequen: Reading what is in the amber

Amber turns up in household waste with an insect caught inside it, and that insect is carrying the blood of whatever it last fed on. Hold a piece and it will tell you what that was, if it is anything you would recognise.

\
\
A Teardown Workbench cannot get it out. That bench takes things apart with hand tools, and what is in the amber is not a part. The Sequencer is a powered block instead: feed it FE and a piece of stamped amber and it reads the DNA out, leaving an Idea Fragment that names the creature. The stone does not survive it - the amber has to be broken up to reach what is inside - so what comes out beside the fragment is a heap of dull chips. It is not waste.

\
\
It takes one piece at a time and nothing can pipe into it or pull out of it - you stand at it. Jade will show you what it is holding, what it is drawing, and how far through it is.

Four fragments of the same creature craft into a Blueprint, the way any four fragments do. Fragments for different creatures will not stack together, so getting four to match is most of the work.

\
\
That sheet is the only thing that says which egg you want, which makes this the one recipe in the game where a Blueprint goes into the grid rather than into your pocket. Lay it in the middle at the Scrap Crafting Table with Glass Shards around it and Rendered Organics beneath, and you get the spawn egg for whatever the resin was carrying.

\
\
The sheet is not spent. It comes back out of the grid, and it will make that egg again for as long as you can find the glass. Nothing else in the world makes a spawn egg.

Spent Amber is what is left after the stone has been broken up to get at what was inside: chips and grit with the life taken out of them. No amount of heat will put it back together, and grinding it further does nothing - whatever made it clear and soft dried out of it a very long time ago, and that is not a thing you can undo.

\
\
You can put it back. Turpentine is the part that left, and tins of it turn up in the rubbish. One heap of chips and one tin, together at any bench, make a lump of fresh resin.

\
\
From there it goes the ordinary way: nine lumps to a block, and a lump in a furnace for a brick. Nothing else in this world produces resin at all, so everything made of it comes back through here.
